parts.text: # SYNTHETIC S01: Query expansion for English museum evidence retrieval

SYNTHETIC BENCHMARK MANUSCRIPT. This is entirely fictional research, not a real publication. All datasets, scores, confidence intervals, costs, examples, and study outcomes are invented. No DOI, real author attribution, or real-world evidence claim is made. The ten page markers represent page-equivalent sections in a long Markdown document, not a typeset PDF.
## Page 01 of 10 — Research question and domain

This fictional study asks whether entity-aware query expansion changes Recall@10 when a retrieval-augmented system processes English questions about museum collection descriptions. The question is deliberately narrow: it concerns evidence use within ArchiveQA-Sim, rather than the reliability of an unrestricted assistant. A record in this collection represents one museum object record; it is not a person, institution, or actual publication. The evaluation set contains 1840 questions and the frozen collection contains 12600 records. We examine a specific comparison with single-pass dense retrieval, keeping the evidence budget at ten retrieved records. The domain was chosen because monthly catalog revisions make document identity and validity relevant to retrieval. A useful system must identify supporting material, preserve its qualifications, and distinguish a missing observation from a negative result. Those requirements determine the analysis rather than an assumption that every pipeline change is beneficial.

The motivating failure is expansion of ambiguous curator surnames. In this setting a superficially relevant passage can contain the correct words while referring to an incompatible object, version, or condition. The intervention therefore uses a museum-specific entity lexicon as a constraint on evidence selection. The constraint is intended to alter the available support, not to rewrite the underlying source statements. We separate the proposition that a candidate was retrieved from the stronger proposition that an answer is justified. This distinction matters for Recall@10, whose operational definition addresses only the outcome specified in this paper. We do not substitute a favorable result on that outcome for measurements of every downstream property. In particular, answer faithfulness was not measured, so conclusions about that property remain outside the observed evidence.

The paper contributes a complete fictional evaluation protocol, an auditable comparison between two fixed pipelines, and a discussion of conditions under which the headline result fails to generalize. Its contribution is not a newly discovered empirical fact about real organizations. All scores, intervals, datasets, case descriptions, and resource measurements were authored as benchmark material. Within this controlled narrative, the important research distinction is between the primary aggregate and the prespecified subgroup of noisy curator-name queries. The latter is retained even when it makes the overall interpretation less attractive. We also keep the collection's rare exhibition objects visible in the analysis, because an aggregate can obscure who or what receives weaker evidence. The resulting report should state both the measured pattern and the uncertainty around it without converting either into a universal ranking.

A working answer to the research question requires several connected observations. First, the source collection must be identifiable and frozen so that citations refer to the same text in both conditions. Second, the comparison needs an explicit unit of analysis and a consistent scoring rule. Third, the reader must know how Recall@10 behaves: for this metric, higher values are better under the definition used here. Finally, the evidence must preserve disconfirming cases rather than averaging them away. We evaluate those requirements in the context of ArchiveQA-Sim and its English material. A finding from this study is consequently conditional on that collection, the selected questions, the chosen evidence budget, and the implementation of entity-aware query expansion. It is not evidence that unrelated languages, data sources, or outcome definitions behave similarly.
## Page 02 of 10 — Collection construction and update history

The ArchiveQA-Sim collection was constructed from fictional museum collection descriptions, with each museum object record assigned a stable local identifier. Authors generated internally consistent versions, including a small set of deliberate conflicts between a current statement and an older statement. The update schedule follows monthly catalog revisions. We retain both the text and its version relationship because deleting an older item would hide an important retrieval challenge. The frozen benchmark release includes 12600 records. Each record is associated with a domain label, a version marker, and a set of question links maintained in the annotation ledger. None of those identifiers denotes a real repository. Their purpose is to let a reviewer trace a claim to its exact synthetic context and distinguish a retrieval error from a change in the source material itself.

Question construction begins with a desired information need rather than with a system-generated answer. Authors then write several surface forms that preserve the same need while varying lexical overlap with the source. For English, this includes appropriate spelling, morphology, and domain-specific expressions. Cases in rare exhibition objects are represented explicitly instead of being merged into the dominant topic group. Questions that require information outside the frozen text are marked as unanswerable under the corpus-only policy. Those cases help distinguish warranted abstention from a failure to retrieve available evidence. The protocol does not allow external browsing to repair a difficult question. Otherwise the two pipelines could silently receive different evidence, and an apparent improvement could reflect access to an additional source rather than the specified retrieval intervention.

The collection includes challenging but plausible distractors. A distractor shares an entity, label, or topic with the relevant museum object record, while differing in the condition that makes the answer applicable. Some distractors are obsolete after an update; others describe a neighboring case. The authors retain these distinctions in the source text so that an exact quotation can expose a scope error. The most important distractor family concerns expansion of ambiguous curator surnames. A robust extraction should report why the source does or does not apply, including qualifying words that are easy to omit in a compressed summary. A citation to a document title alone is insufficient for this purpose. The relevant evidence is the local statement together with its adjacent qualification, version note, or exception.

Corpus preparation freezes the bytes before any pipeline is evaluated. The ledger records a content digest and the identifier of the relevant source location. Corrections after freezing create a new release rather than silently modifying the version already evaluated. This procedure makes a later replication possible without assuming that a live document has remained unchanged. It also exposes the limited scope of the benchmark: ArchiveQA-Sim represents authored text, not a sample of every English information service. Coverage of rare exhibition objects does not guarantee coverage of every difficult case. We therefore report the composition and update process as study conditions. A secondary analysis may explore different collections, but it would answer an additional question and could not retroactively expand the scope of the present primary comparison.

Consider a fictional visitor asking which exhibition first displayed an object catalogued under an abbreviated curator surname. The source collection contains a contemporary exhibition note and a later retrospective description. The retrospective uses the modern spelling of the surname, while the contemporary note records an earlier abbreviation. A naive expansion can improve lexical overlap with the retrospective and still miss the event that the visitor actually asked about. The entity lexicon helps distinguish a curator from an artist, but it cannot infer a missing historical relationship from surname similarity alone. For this reason, annotation records the object, exhibition context, and temporal qualifier as separate pieces of support. A retrieved retrospective is a plausible distractor rather than automatically correct evidence. The case also explains why noisy curator-name queries need separate reporting: their difficulty concerns identity resolution, which differs from retrieving ordinary descriptive terms. The example is an authored illustration of the mechanism and is not an additional measured query result. It provides no frequency estimate for curator-name ambiguity. Its scientific purpose is to show which source qualification would have to survive retrieval before an answer about the first exhibition could be justified.
## Page 03 of 10 — Study design and comparison

The study uses a randomized query-level controlled experiment. The intervention condition implements entity-aware query expansion; the reference condition implements single-pass dense retrieval. Both conditions operate on the same frozen release of ArchiveQA-Sim and receive the same question definitions. The design determines which causal language is appropriate. Assignment supports a narrow causal interpretation of the specified software contrast within this controlled evaluation; it does not establish downstream real-world effects. It remains necessary to specify what was actually changed, because even an assigned software intervention cannot establish the effects of an unmeasured organizational policy. We keep source access, question wording, and the scoring rubric fixed wherever the design permits. The comparison is evaluated at the level defined in the protocol rather than by selecting attractive examples after observing the output. This makes the aggregate result interpretable within the stated design while leaving its external validity open.

Implementation order is logged so that a change in a cached resource does not masquerade as an intervention effect. Each run records the source release, retrieval configuration, relevant museum object record identifiers, and the allowed evidence budget of ten retrieved records. When an answer cannot be grounded in the permitted material, the pipeline may abstain according to the shared rule. The decision to abstain is stored separately from the final outcome score. This distinction is needed because a cautious system can change the mix of attempted questions, and the score can become misleading if only successful attempts are retained. All eligible questions stay in the declared analysis set. Exclusions are defined by protocol violations such as corrupted source text, never by whether a pipeline happened to perform poorly on a case.

The investigators identify collection age as a material threat to interpretation. The handling of that threat follows the stated design and is not assumed to make every group exchangeable. We describe the observed context alongside the score difference so that a review can retain uncertainty about alternative explanations. The intervention also interacts with the question stratum: noisy curator-name queries are not interchangeable with ordinary questions. The subgroup was specified before the scores were summarized, and its result is reported regardless of its direction. This avoids presenting an aggregate benefit as evidence of an improvement for each subset. The analysis should therefore distinguish the primary contrast, the subgroup contrast, and any illustrative cases used to explain the mechanism. They are related observations with different evidential roles.

The protocol requires the two conditions to keep the same output policy and the same definition of a supported answer. A pipeline is not permitted to manufacture a source statement merely because it retrieves a more convenient record. The source text remains authoritative when it contradicts the generated answer. Investigators inspect examples containing a nearby catalog note, since a short excerpt can appear persuasive after the limiting sentence is removed. These inspections inform the error taxonomy, but they do not replace the full scoring set. A collection of favorable examples would not estimate Recall@10. Conversely, a negative example can reveal a real failure mode without showing how common that failure is. We preserve both types of evidence and state which conclusions depend on aggregate scoring rather than on qualitative inspection.
## Page 04 of 10 — Pipeline and evidence handling

The reference pipeline begins with single-pass dense retrieval. It constructs a candidate set from the frozen collection and applies a fixed selection policy before producing the evaluated output. The intervention replaces the relevant evidence-selection component with entity-aware query expansion. Inputs and source releases are otherwise kept aligned within the constraints of the study design. Both conditions use ten retrieved records, so an improvement cannot be explained merely by granting one condition an unlimited number of source passages. The intervention must work within that budget. Candidate provenance remains attached to every selected passage, allowing investigators to distinguish the passage that influenced an answer from an incidental item that happened to appear in the retrieval log. This separation matters when the correct document contains several incompatible local statements.

Evidence assembly preserves the smallest complete context that can support or refute an answer. In particular, a quantitative value must remain connected to its unit, population, and relevant qualification. Where a table contains the relevant value, its caption and notes accompany the selected cells. A nearby catalog note is included when it changes applicability. This rule prevents a mechanically correct quotation from acquiring a broader meaning during summarization. The failure family of expansion of ambiguous curator surnames illustrates why this additional context is necessary. We do not treat quotation matching as sufficient proof of scientific support. It establishes that words appeared in the source, whereas the question of whether those words support the whole claim requires a separate contextual judgment.

The intervention uses a museum-specific entity lexicon to narrow the interpretation of candidate evidence. That safeguard is configured before the held-out comparison and cannot be tuned separately on each failed evaluation question. Investigators document situations in which the safeguard removes a distractor and situations in which it suppresses useful evidence. The latter category is especially relevant for noisy curator-name queries. A restrictive policy can improve average relevance while reducing recall for unusual language, rare concepts, or ambiguous identifiers. The protocol consequently records rejected candidates and the reason for rejection, rather than retaining only the final output. Those records permit a later analysis of whether the intervention's apparent benefit depends on a shift in the types of questions it is willing or able to answer.

A trace consists of the question identifier, source release, candidate identities, selected evidence, output, and scoring decision. It is an auditable record of the fictional computation, not a transcript of private model reasoning. Investigators can replay the evidence selection from the frozen inputs without requiring access to an author's internal explanation. Repeated executions use seed 1101 where a deterministic ordering is required. A different seed may be explored in sensitivity analysis, but the declared result is not chosen from the most favorable execution. The trace also distinguishes a missing measurement from a measured zero. If a resource field is absent, no arithmetic can recover its value from the answer score alone. The source must report the measurement before a review can make a quantitative claim about it.
## Page 05 of 10 — Annotation and primary outcome

The primary endpoint is Recall@10. Under the operational definition used for ArchiveQA-Sim, higher values indicate better performance. The score belongs to a defined evaluation task and should not be substituted for a different retrieval or answer-quality measure. In particular, ranking metrics depend on their cutoff and relevance judgments, while answer-level measures depend on how output claims are evaluated. A literature synthesis should preserve the metric name exactly, including a cutoff where present. Renaming every outcome as generic accuracy would remove information needed to judge comparability. We report the baseline score, intervention score, and intervention-minus-baseline contrast on the metric's native scale. These values are not relative percentage changes, and no unit conversion is implied by their decimal representation.

Annotators inspect the relevant museum object record and its local context before assigning a label. Their task is to decide whether the requested information is supported under the source's stated conditions. They mark contradictory passages explicitly and do not resolve a conflict simply by choosing the sentence that matches the generated answer. For English questions, language-specific expressions are evaluated in context instead of being translated into an easier benchmark question. A disagreement record includes the competing interpretations and the source location needed to resolve them. Consensus labels are frozen before the compared output is summarized. This process reduces one source of outcome-dependent annotation, but it does not eliminate the limitations of an authored benchmark or establish that the rubric captures every dimension of practical usefulness.

The scoring ledger contains all 1840 eligible questions. The score summary retains the distinction between overall performance and the prespecified subgroup of noisy curator-name queries. Questions are not duplicated in the overall result simply because they appear in an explanatory case study. A single example may illustrate several error categories, but its evaluation weight follows the original analysis unit. This avoids inflating confidence by counting a rhetorically useful case multiple times. When the underlying design creates dependence between observations, uncertainty is computed at the corresponding grouping level. The paper reports uncertainty as a ninety-five percent confidence interval for the score contrast. An interval crossing zero is not described as proof of no effect; it indicates that the reported analysis does not clearly separate the contrast from zero.

Annotation quality is examined through a structured review of disagreements, ambiguous question wording, and omitted source qualifications. The most consequential errors arise when a passage is relevant to the topic but supports a different version or condition. This concern links the rubric to expansion of ambiguous curator surnames. Investigators ask whether the output retained the decisive catalog note, whether it attributed the result to the correct source release, and whether it overstated what the evidence could establish. These checks are not additional favorable outcomes that may replace the prespecified primary endpoint. They explain the interpretation of Recall@10 and identify threats to validity. The missing measurement of answer faithfulness remains missing after this exercise, since checking source support does not automatically measure every downstream outcome.
## Page 06 of 10 — Primary results and interval interpretation

The primary results are as follows. Baseline Recall@10 was 0.684, and intervention Recall@10 was 0.752. The intervention-minus-baseline difference was +0.068, with a ninety-five percent confidence interval from +0.041 to +0.095. These numbers refer to the aggregate evaluation on ArchiveQA-Sim. They do not describe the subgroup, another dataset, or a different language. The interval excludes zero in the favorable direction for this endpoint, under the declared analysis assumptions. The magnitude remains a contrast on the metric's native scale. We do not convert this contrast into a universal percentage improvement across retrieval systems. A review that reports the favorable direction while omitting the interval would lose information about precision. A review that changes the sign convention would also reverse the interpretation of outcomes for which lower values are preferable.

Table 1 provides the principal numerical comparison in a form suitable for exact checking. The caption identifies the data release and the metric, and the notes define the contrast as intervention minus baseline. The subgroup row is included in the same table so that a reader cannot reasonably infer uniform benefit from the aggregate alone. Both rows are reported under the original protocol. The table does not contain a measurement of answer faithfulness, nor can such a measurement be inferred from its score columns. Any source-based summary should retain the native metric, the contrast direction, the interval, and the target population of questions. A cell copied without the caption or notes could be numerically accurate yet semantically incomplete.

A numerical contrast can be compatible with several mechanisms. In ArchiveQA-Sim, qualitative traces suggest that entity-aware query expansion changes which museum object record is selected and how its qualifications survive evidence assembly. This pattern is consistent with the intended intervention, but the interpretation remains bounded by the randomized query-level controlled experiment. The assigned comparison concerns the specified software component, and extrapolation to other mechanisms or practical outcomes would exceed what was assigned. A plausible narrative does not repair a design limitation. We therefore separate the reported score change from a broader claim that the intervention is the sole cause of a practical improvement. The result also does not imply that single-pass dense retrieval is universally inferior: the reference pipeline may behave differently under another corpus composition, update schedule, or evidence budget. Those counterfactual settings were not measured here.

The numerical summary is deliberately accompanied by uncertainty rather than by a binary declaration of success. The confidence interval describes the precision of the specified contrast under the analysis assumptions. It does not certify that every question improved, that every rare case was protected, or that the system will maintain the same behavior after monthly catalog revisions. Nor does a favorable aggregate justify replacing the subgroup result with the overall average. The relevant scientific conclusion is conditional: this comparison estimates a particular difference in Recall@10 for the declared English collection and evaluation protocol. Claims about deployment utility would additionally require the missing measurement of answer faithfulness and evidence about conditions beyond the present fictional corpus.
Table 1. Primary and prespecified subgroup outcomes for ArchiveQA-Sim using Recall@10.

| Evaluation set | Baseline | Intervention | Difference | 95% CI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All eligible questions | 0.684 | 0.752 | +0.068 | [+0.041, +0.095] |
| noisy curator-name queries | 0.610 | 0.600 | -0.010 | [-0.040, +0.020] |

Table 1 notes. Difference means intervention minus baseline on the native Recall@10 scale; higher is better. Intervals are ninety-five percent confidence intervals for the contrast, not intervals for the separate condition means. A subgroup interval containing zero does not establish absence of harm or a clear subgroup benefit.
## Page 07 of 10 — Subgroup counterevidence and unexpected findings

The prespecified subgroup consists of noisy curator-name queries. Its baseline Recall@10 was 0.610, and its intervention score was 0.600. The subgroup contrast was -0.010, with a ninety-five percent confidence interval from -0.040 to +0.020. The subgroup interval includes zero; the study does not establish a clear subgroup benefit. This observation must be retained beside the aggregate result. It is not an acceptable summary to state that every query benefited when this row is null or adverse. The subgroup also illustrates why a study can offer supporting evidence for a general mechanism while simultaneously providing counterevidence to a stronger, universal claim. The two observations are scientifically compatible when their scopes are stated explicitly.

The unexpected finding was the persistence of expansion of ambiguous curator surnames despite the addition of a museum-specific entity lexicon. Investigators had expected this safeguard to resolve the relevant ambiguity more reliably. Traces showed that a structurally valid selection could still be wrong when the question depended on a distinction that the candidate representation did not preserve. The error was not simply a missing keyword. In some cases, the relevant evidence was present but lost a qualification during the passage-to-answer transition. This finding motivates a cautious interpretation of mechanism-based explanations: an intervention may address a known failure family while leaving a narrower variant unresolved. The study records this limitation instead of silently changing the definition of success after seeing the evaluation outputs.

The subgroup analysis is not used to claim that an adverse pattern occurs in every underrepresented setting. Its scope is the declared set of noisy curator-name queries in ArchiveQA-Sim. Other rare or difficult questions may involve different mechanisms. We keep that limitation explicit because an attractive synthesis can overgeneralize counterevidence just as easily as it can overgeneralize a benefit. A null interval is also not evidence that the intervention is harmless. It leaves uncertainty about effects of a size compatible with the reported interval. For a deployment decision, that uncertainty may be relevant even when the primary aggregate has a favorable direction. The present paper supplies the comparison and its bounds, rather than a universal rule for adopting or rejecting the intervention.

Error inspection distinguishes source absence, candidate-selection failure, context loss, and unsupported answer formulation. The distinction matters because these categories suggest different remedies. If the corpus lacks a relevant statement, a more elaborate reranker cannot create valid evidence. If the relevant passage is retrieved but its catalog note is dropped, increasing retrieval recall may leave the central problem unchanged. If the output makes a claim that no selected passage supports, an exact source identifier does not rescue the claim. These observations contribute practical diagnostic structure without adding an unmeasured performance endpoint. In particular, they do not establish the missing outcome of answer faithfulness. The most defensible synthesis preserves the unexpected failure and the boundary of the available measurements together.

The mechanism diagnosis connects this study's domain illustration to the quantitative contrast without treating the illustration as another data point. For ArchiveQA-Sim, the investigators follow the information need from the original English wording through candidate selection, local context assembly, and the scored output. They ask at which transition expansion of ambiguous curator surnames becomes possible, which condition the intervention actually enforces, and which condition remains implicit. This diagnostic sequence is useful because the same final error can arise through different routes. An excluded correct candidate requires a different remedy from a retrieved candidate whose limiting note was lost. A failed source-version check also differs from a well-versioned source that never contains the requested fact. The records therefore preserve both the selected museum object record and the rejected alternatives needed to inspect the decision boundary. They do not record a fictional success simply because a museum-specific entity lexicon was enabled. The prespecified subgroup of noisy curator-name queries supplies an empirical boundary within this authored protocol, whereas the case narrative supplies a possible explanation that remains open to further testing. A review should identify that difference in evidential role. It may connect the mechanism to the pattern as an interpretation, provided it does not turn the interpretation into an additional measured result. The same restraint applies to answer faithfulness: diagnostic detail cannot create an outcome measurement that the protocol omitted. This separation between traceable facts, mechanism hypotheses, and unavailable information is essential for retaining counterevidence in a compressed integrated account.
## Page 08 of 10 — Resource accounting and unavailable measurements

Resource accounting is reported separately from Recall@10. Monetary cost was not measured in either condition. The baseline cost, intervention cost, and cost difference are unknown, not zero. Table 2 preserves this distinction between the score outcome and resource observations. The interpretation cannot be reversed by assuming that a compact pipeline is free or that an additional component must be expensive. Both assumptions would require measurements absent from the relevant source. Where a monetary value is reported, its unit is United States dollars per query under the fictional accounting boundary. It does not represent a total organizational budget, an estimate of staffing costs, or a claim about a live provider's price. The resource section consequently states the accounting boundary before discussing efficiency, and keeps unavailable fields explicitly unavailable.

The measurement boundary determines what a resource number means. A per-query charge can include the components specified by the fictional logging protocol while excluding work performed outside the recorded request. A review should not extrapolate from such a value to lifetime cost without assumptions about query volume, maintenance, staffing, and changes in the source collection. The schedule of monthly catalog revisions is relevant because rebuilding evidence or invalidating a cache can move work between requests and maintenance periods. Our primary score does not measure that moved work. We therefore avoid converting the score difference into a cost-effectiveness ratio when its denominator is not adequately observed. A missing resource observation is an evidence gap that should remain visible in both the per-paper analysis and the integrated review.

The study did not measure answer faithfulness. This is an explicit limitation, not a statement that the corresponding quantity was zero, unchanged, or irrelevant. The absence also cannot be repaired by citing a different paper that evaluated a distinct outcome under another design. Such a citation might inform a broader discussion, but it would not make the present source contain a measurement it never reported. We treat this boundary as part of the study's scientific content. An extraction system should distinguish not reported from a null result supported by an interval. The subgroup contrast is an example of a reported uncertain or adverse result; the unavailable outcome is an example of information that was never obtained within the protocol.

Efficiency claims require a joint description of resources, performance, and workload. For ArchiveQA-Sim, the workload consists of 1840 declared questions against 12600 frozen records, with ten retrieved records supplied to the downstream stage. Those conditions should accompany any attempt to compare resource figures. A system serving a different language mix, a larger collection, or a more demanding evidence policy could have a different resource profile even if its score were similar. We report the observed accounting status and leave the unobserved components unresolved. This restraint is especially important in a synthetic benchmark: plausible numerical detail should never be mistaken for a measurement of an actual service. All resource values in this manuscript are fictional controlled facts for evaluating source-grounded review behavior.
Table 2. Resource accounting and unavailable measurements in ArchiveQA-Sim.

| Quantity | Baseline | Intervention | Interpretation boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Monetary cost, USD/query | not measured | not measured | Fictional per-query accounting only |
| answer faithfulness | not measured | not measured | No zero or null result may be inferred |
| Evidence budget | ten retrieved records | ten retrieved records | Fixed within this study |

Table 2 notes. Not measured means the quantity was unavailable under this protocol; it must not be replaced with zero. A per-query monetary observation, when present, excludes unspecified staffing and maintenance costs. None of these numbers reports a live vendor price or a real organization's operating expenditure.
## Page 09 of 10 — Validity, applicability, and reproducibility

Internal validity is bounded by the randomized query-level controlled experiment and the way the authored collection represents museum collection descriptions. The principal named threat is collection age. The paper describes that threat because it offers an alternative explanation or a boundary condition relevant to the observed contrast. A source-grounded review should not remove the threat when compressing the method into a short label. Nor should it infer that a particular adjustment makes all unobserved differences disappear. We preserve the exact design description and the distinction between the primary analysis and exploratory interpretation. The result remains evidence about the stated comparison, not a license to assert every causal pathway that could plausibly connect retrieval to a useful downstream decision.

External validity requires caution because the collection, questions, and update process are all authored. The English material in ArchiveQA-Sim does not establish coverage of languages that were not evaluated. The presence of rare exhibition objects in the benchmark also does not prove that the dataset represents every minority use case. The most relevant applicability conditions are the collection's museum object record structure, its update schedule, the evidence budget, and the use of a museum-specific entity lexicon. If any of those conditions changes, the proposed mechanism may interact differently with the input. We therefore report these conditions alongside the numerical result. They allow a later reader to assess similarity to a new task without pretending that a single fictional evaluation has already tested that task.

Cross-paper numerical ranking is not justified by the information in this study alone. Recall, reciprocal rank, normalized discounted gain, answer F1, citation precision, factual consistency, freshness, attribution coverage, and calibration scores have different meanings and scales. Even two studies using the same label may apply different question populations or annotation policies. A review can compare methods and limitations across such studies, but it should not announce a winning system by sorting the raw score values. For Recall@10, the declared favorable direction is higher; changing that direction would itself create an error. The appropriate comparison is between this paper's intervention and reference condition under ArchiveQA-Sim, with the uncertainty and subgroup evidence preserved.

Reproducibility is supported by stable local identifiers, frozen source digests, deterministic generation seed 1101, and a complete statement of the synthetic protocol. None of these features converts the study into a real publication. They make the benchmark internally auditable so that an extraction or verification system can be checked against known facts. A replication of the fictional evaluation should report whether it used the same corpus release and scoring definition before comparing its output. A literature-review benchmark should additionally record which parts of each source were read and which claims were ultimately cited. Coverage of every source part and support for every delivered claim are complementary obligations. Completing one does not automatically satisfy the other, and both should remain measurable in the resulting artifacts.
## Page 10 of 10 — Interpretation and bounded conclusions

The aggregate comparison estimates an intervention-minus-baseline difference of +0.068 in Recall@10, with a ninety-five percent confidence interval from +0.041 to +0.095. That statement is the primary quantitative conclusion for ArchiveQA-Sim. Its interpretation is conditional on the declared English workload and the randomized query-level controlled experiment. The subgroup of noisy curator-name queries has a different contrast, -0.010, with interval -0.040 to +0.020. The two results should appear together in an evidence table. A summary that reports only the aggregate, or silently replaces the subgroup with the overall average, would erase relevant counterevidence. We consequently conclude with a bounded account of what was measured and where the apparent advantage or uncertainty does not support a stronger statement.

The mechanism discussion identifies entity-aware query expansion as a way to change evidence selection under monthly catalog revisions. The discussion also identifies expansion of ambiguous curator surnames as an unresolved or incompletely resolved challenge. These observations can motivate a new evaluation of the safeguard, but they do not establish that the problem has been solved. Further work should predefine a question set that isolates the suspected mechanism and preserve the local source context needed to judge errors. A future experiment could test whether a modified a museum-specific entity lexicon changes the subgroup result. It would need to report its own comparison rather than treating the present result as a forecast. The current manuscript neither supplies those future measurements nor fills the gap in answer faithfulness.

For a corpus-only literature review, the relevant synthesis should connect methods, evaluated outcomes, source conditions, counterevidence, resource status, and study limitations. It should make clear which statements are direct source facts and which are interpretations formed across studies. Direct facts from this manuscript include the score pair, confidence interval, subgroup result, design, language, and accounting status. An integrated interpretation may discuss recurring mechanisms, but its scope must follow the evidence actually available across the included papers. Unmeasured quantities should remain unknown, and observational comparisons should retain their causal limitations. This is particularly important when papers use different datasets or native metrics, since a smooth narrative can otherwise hide the conditions that make their results incomparable.

In conclusion, ArchiveQA-Sim supplies a fictional, fully specified case for evaluating whether an automated review preserves scientific qualifications while handling a document of substantial length. The substantive content is distributed across the entire manuscript rather than concentrated only in an abstract. Methods, update conditions, endpoint definitions, adverse or null subgroup evidence, resource status, and validity limits all contribute to the final interpretation. The intended reading task therefore requires more than locating a headline score. It requires retaining the evidence needed to support a precise statement and rejecting stronger assertions that the source cannot justify. The manuscript is explicitly synthetic benchmark material, with no real authors, real dataset release, clinical recommendation, legal finding, or external publication claim.

questions.text: Across these synthetic studies, what effects and counterevidence are reported for retrieval and RAG interventions under their stated designs and native metrics?
How do language, dataset updates, resource measurements, and validity limitations constrain interpretation and cross-study comparisons?

Further work should predefine a question set that isolates the suspected mechanism and preserve the local source context needed to judge errors. For a corpus-only literature review, the relevant synthesis should connect methods, evaluated outcomes, source conditions, counterevidence, resource status, and study limitations. It should make clear which statements are direct source facts and which are interpretations formed across studies. Direct facts from this manuscript include the score pair, confidence interval, subgroup result, design, language, and accounting status. Unmeasured quantities should remain unknown, and observational comparisons should retain their causal limitations. The substantive content is distributed across the entire manuscript rather than concentrated only in an abstract. Methods, update conditions, endpoint definitions, adverse or null subgroup evidence, resource status, and validity limits all contribute to the final interpretation. The intended reading task therefore requires more than locating a headline score. It requires retaining the evidence needed to support a precise statement and rejecting stronger assertions that the source cannot justify. The frozen benchmark release includes 12600 records. Each record is associated with a domain label, a version marker, and a set of question links maintained in the annotation ledger. None of those identifiers denotes a real repository. Their purpose is to let a reviewer trace a claim to its exact synthetic context and distinguish a retrieval error from a change in the source material itself.

Question construction begins with a desired information need rather than with a system-generated answer. Authors then write several surface forms that preserve the same need while varying lexical overlap with the source. For English, this includes appropriate spelling, morphology, and domain-specific expressions. Cases in rare exhibition objects are represented explicitly instead of being merged into the dominant topic group. Questions that require information outside the frozen text are marked as unanswerable under the corpus-only policy. Those cases help distinguish warranted abstention from a failure to retrieve available evidence. The protocol does not allow external browsing to repair a difficult question. Otherwise the two pipelines could silently receive different evidence, and an apparent improvement could reflect access to an additional source rather than the specified retrieval intervention.

The collection includes challenging but plausible distractors. A distractor shares an entity, label, or topic with the relevant museum object record, while differing in the condition that makes the answer applicable. Some distractors are obsolete after an update; others describe a neighboring case. The authors retain these distinctions in the source text so that an exact quotation can expose a scope error. The most important distractor family concerns expansion of ambiguous curator surnames. A robust extraction should report why the source does or does not apply, including qualifying words that are easy to omit in a compressed summary. A citation to a document title alone is insufficient for this purpose. The relevant evidence is the local statement together with its adjacent qualification, version note, or exception.

Corpus preparation freezes the bytes before any pipeline is evaluated. The ledger records a content digest and the identifier of the relevant source location. Corrections after freezing create a new release rather than silently modifying the version already evaluated. This procedure makes a later replication possible without assuming that a live document has remained unchanged. It also exposes the limited scope of the benchmark: ArchiveQA-Sim represents authored text, not a sample of every English information service. Coverage of rare exhibition objects does not guarantee coverage of every difficult case. We therefore report the composition and update process as study conditions. A secondary analysis may explore different collections, but it would answer an additional question and could not retroactively expand the scope of the present primary comparison.

Consider a fictional visitor asking which exhibition first displayed an object catalogued under an abbreviated curator surname. The source collection contains a contemporary exhibition note and a later retrospective description. The retrospective uses the modern spelling of the surname, while the contemporary note records an earlier abbreviation. A naive expansion can improve lexical overlap with the retrospective and still miss the event that the visitor actually asked about. The entity lexicon helps distinguish a curator from an artist, but it cannot infer a missing historical relationship from surname similarity alone. For this reason, annotation records the object, exhibition context, and temporal qualifier as separate pieces of support. A retrieved retrospective is a plausible distractor rather than automatically correct evidence. The case also explains why noisy curator-name queries need separate reporting: their difficulty concerns identity resolution, which differs from retrieving ordinary descriptive terms. The example is an authored illustration of the mechanism and is not an additional measured query result. It provides no frequency estimate for curator-name ambiguity. Its scientific purpose is to show which source qualification would have to survive retrieval before an answer about the first exhibition could be justified.

The study uses a randomized query-level controlled experiment. The intervention condition implements entity-aware query expansion; the reference condition implements single-pass dense retrieval. Both conditions operate on the same frozen release of ArchiveQA-Sim and receive the same question definitions. The design determines which causal language is appropriate. Assignment supports a narrow causal interpretation of the specified software contrast within this controlled evaluation; it does not establish downstream real-world effects. It remains necessary to specify what was actually changed, because even an assigned software intervention cannot establish the effects of an unmeasured organizational policy. We keep source access, question wording, and the scoring rubric fixed wherever the design permits. The comparison is evaluated at the level defined in the protocol rather than by selecting attractive examples after observing the output. This makes the aggregate result interpretable within the stated design while leaving its external validity open.

Implementation order is logged so that a change in a cached resource does not masquerade as an intervention effect. Each run records the source release, retrieval configuration, relevant museum object record identifiers, and the allowed evidence budget of ten retrieved records. When an answer cannot be grounded in the permitted material, the pipeline may abstain according to the shared rule. The decision to abstain is stored separately from the final outcome score. This distinction is needed because a cautious system can change the mix of attempted questions, and the score can become misleading if only successful attempts are retained. All eligible questions stay in the declared analysis set. Exclusions are defined by protocol violations such as corrupted source text, never by whether a pipeline happened to perform poorly on a case.

The investigators identify collection age as a material threat to interpretation. The handling of that threat follows the stated design and is not assumed to make every group exchangeable. We describe the observed context alongside the score difference so that a review can retain uncertainty about alternative explanations. The intervention also interacts with the question stratum: noisy curator-name queries are not interchangeable with ordinary questions. The subgroup was specified before the scores were summarized, and its result is reported regardless of its direction. This avoids presenting an aggregate benefit as evidence of an improvement for each subset. The analysis should therefore distinguish the primary contrast, the subgroup contrast, and any illustrative cases used to explain the mechanism. They are related observations with different evidential roles.

The protocol requires the two conditions to keep the same output policy and the same definition of a supported answer. A pipeline is not permitted to manufacture a source statement merely because it retrieves a more convenient record. The source text remains authoritative when it contradicts the generated answer. Investigators inspect examples containing a nearby catalog note, since a short excerpt can appear persuasive after the limiting sentence is removed. These inspections inform the error taxonomy, but they do not replace the full scoring set. A collection of favorable examples would not estimate Recall@10. Conversely, a negative example can reveal a real failure mode without showing how common that failure is. We preserve both types of evidence and state which conclusions depend on aggregate scoring rather than on qualitative inspection.

The reference pipeline begins with single-pass dense retrieval. It constructs a candidate set from the frozen collection and applies a fixed selection policy before producing the evaluated output. The intervention replaces the relevant evidence-selection component with entity-aware query expansion. Inputs and source releases are otherwise kept aligned within the constraints of the study design. Both conditions use ten retrieved records, so an improvement cannot be explained merely by granting one condition an unlimited number of source passages. The intervention must work within that budget. Candidate provenance remains attached to every selected passage, allowing investigators to distinguish the passage that influenced an answer from an incidental item that happened to appear in the retrieval log. This separation matters when the correct document contains several incompatible local statements.

Evidence assembly preserves the smallest complete context that can support or refute an answer. In particular, a quantitative value must remain connected to its unit, population, and relevant qualification. Where a table contains the relevant value, its caption and notes accompany the selected cells. A nearby catalog note is included when it changes applicability. This rule prevents a mechanically correct quotation from acquiring a broader meaning during summarization. The failure family of expansion of ambiguous curator surnames illustrates why this additional context is necessary. We do not treat quotation matching as sufficient proof of scientific support. It establishes that words appeared in the source, whereas the question of whether those words support the whole claim requires a separate contextual judgment.

The intervention uses a museum-specific entity lexicon to narrow the interpretation of candidate evidence. That safeguard is configured before the held-out comparison and cannot be tuned separately on each failed evaluation question. Investigators document situations in which the safeguard removes a distractor and situations in which it suppresses useful evidence. The latter category is especially relevant for noisy curator-name queries. A restrictive policy can improve average relevance while reducing recall for unusual language, rare concepts, or ambiguous identifiers. The protocol consequently records rejected candidates and the reason for rejection, rather than retaining only the final output. Those records permit a later analysis of whether the intervention's apparent benefit depends on a shift in the types of questions it is willing or able to answer.

A trace consists of the question identifier, source release, candidate identities, selected evidence, output, and scoring decision. It is an auditable record of the fictional computation, not a transcript of private model reasoning. Investigators can replay the evidence selection from the frozen inputs without requiring access to an author's internal explanation. Repeated executions use seed 1101 where a deterministic ordering is required. A different seed may be explored in sensitivity analysis, but the declared result is not chosen from the most favorable execution. The trace also distinguishes a missing measurement from a measured zero. If a resource field is absent, no arithmetic can recover its value from the answer score alone. The source must report the measurement before a review can make a quantitative claim about it.

The primary endpoint is Recall@10. Under the operational definition used for ArchiveQA-Sim, higher values indicate better performance. The score belongs to a defined evaluation task and should not be substituted for a different retrieval or answer-quality measure. In particular, ranking metrics depend on their cutoff and relevance judgments, while answer-level measures depend on how output claims are evaluated. A literature synthesis should preserve the metric name exactly, including a cutoff where present. Renaming every outcome as generic accuracy would remove information needed to judge comparability. We report the baseline score, intervention score, and intervention-minus-baseline contrast on the metric's native scale. These values are not relative percentage changes, and no unit conversion is implied by their decimal representation.

Annotators inspect the relevant museum object record and its local context before assigning a label. Their task is to decide whether the requested information is supported under the source's stated conditions. They mark contradictory passages explicitly and do not resolve a conflict simply by choosing the sentence that matches the generated answer. For English questions, language-specific expressions are evaluated in context instead of being translated into an easier benchmark question. A disagreement record includes the competing interpretations and the source location needed to resolve them. Consensus labels are frozen before the compared output is summarized. This process reduces one source of outcome-dependent annotation, but it does not eliminate the limitations of an authored benchmark or establish that the rubric captures every dimension of practical usefulness.

The scoring ledger contains all 1840 eligible questions. The score summary retains the distinction between overall performance and the prespecified subgroup of noisy curator-name queries. Questions are not duplicated in the overall result simply because they appear in an explanatory case study. A single example may illustrate several error categories, but its evaluation weight follows the original analysis unit. This avoids inflating confidence by counting a rhetorically useful case multiple times. When the underlying design creates dependence between observations, uncertainty is computed at the corresponding grouping level. The paper reports uncertainty as a ninety-five percent confidence interval for the score contrast. An interval crossing zero is not described as proof of no effect; it indicates that the reported analysis does not clearly separate the contrast from zero.

Annotation quality is examined through a structured review of disagreements, ambiguous question wording, and omitted source qualifications. The most consequential errors arise when a passage is relevant to the topic but supports a different version or condition. This concern links the rubric to expansion of ambiguous curator surnames. Investigators ask whether the output retained the decisive catalog note, whether it attributed the result to the correct source release, and whether it overstated what the evidence could establish. These checks are not additional favorable outcomes that may replace the prespecified primary endpoint. They explain the interpretation of Recall@10 and identify threats to validity. The missing measurement of answer faithfulness remains missing after this exercise, since checking source support does not automatically measure every downstream outcome.

The primary results are as follows. Baseline Recall@10 was 0.684, and intervention Recall@10 was 0.752. The intervention-minus-baseline difference was +0.068, with a ninety-five percent confidence interval from +0.041 to +0.095. These numbers refer to the aggregate evaluation on ArchiveQA-Sim. They do not describe the subgroup, another dataset, or a different language. The interval excludes zero in the favorable direction for this endpoint, under the declared analysis assumptions. The magnitude remains a contrast on the metric's native scale. We do not convert this contrast into a universal percentage improvement across retrieval systems. A review that reports the favorable direction while omitting the interval would lose information about precision. A review that changes the sign convention would also reverse the interpretation of outcomes for which lower values are preferable.

| Evaluation set | Baseline | Intervention | Difference | 95% CI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All eligible questions | 0.684 | 0.752 | +0.068 | [+0.041, +0.095] |
| noisy curator-name queries | 0.610 | 0.600 | -0.010 | [-0.040, +0.020] |

Table 1 notes. Difference means intervention minus baseline on the native Recall@10 scale; higher is better. Intervals are ninety-five percent confidence intervals for the contrast, not intervals for the separate condition means. A subgroup interval containing zero does not establish absence of harm or a clear subgroup benefit.

A numerical contrast can be compatible with several mechanisms. In ArchiveQA-Sim, qualitative traces suggest that entity-aware query expansion changes which museum object record is selected and how its qualifications survive evidence assembly. This pattern is consistent with the intended intervention, but the interpretation remains bounded by the randomized query-level controlled experiment. The assigned comparison concerns the specified software component, and extrapolation to other mechanisms or practical outcomes would exceed what was assigned. A plausible narrative does not repair a design limitation. We therefore separate the reported score change from a broader claim that the intervention is the sole cause of a practical improvement. The result also does not imply that single-pass dense retrieval is universally inferior: the reference pipeline may behave differently under another corpus composition, update schedule, or evidence budget. Those counterfactual settings were not measured here.

The numerical summary is deliberately accompanied by uncertainty rather than by a binary declaration of success. The confidence interval describes the precision of the specified contrast under the analysis assumptions. It does not certify that every question improved, that every rare case was protected, or that the system will maintain the same behavior after monthly catalog revisions. Nor does a favorable aggregate justify replacing the subgroup result with the overall average. The relevant scientific conclusion is conditional: this comparison estimates a particular difference in Recall@10 for the declared English collection and evaluation protocol. Claims about deployment utility would additionally require the missing measurement of answer faithfulness and evidence about conditions beyond the present fictional corpus.

The prespecified subgroup consists of noisy curator-name queries. Its baseline Recall@10 was 0.610, and its intervention score was 0.600. The subgroup contrast was -0.010, with a ninety-five percent confidence interval from -0.040 to +0.020. The subgroup interval includes zero; the study does not establish a clear subgroup benefit. This observation must be retained beside the aggregate result. It is not an acceptable summary to state that every query benefited when this row is null or adverse. The subgroup also illustrates why a study can offer supporting evidence for a general mechanism while simultaneously providing counterevidence to a stronger, universal claim. The two observations are scientifically compatible when their scopes are stated explicitly.

The unexpected finding was the persistence of expansion of ambiguous curator surnames despite the addition of a museum-specific entity lexicon. Investigators had expected this safeguard to resolve the relevant ambiguity more reliably. Traces showed that a structurally valid selection could still be wrong when the question depended on a distinction that the candidate representation did not preserve. The error was not simply a missing keyword. In some cases, the relevant evidence was present but lost a qualification during the passage-to-answer transition. This finding motivates a cautious interpretation of mechanism-based explanations: an intervention may address a known failure family while leaving a narrower variant unresolved. The study records this limitation instead of silently changing the definition of success after seeing the evaluation outputs.

The subgroup analysis is not used to claim that an adverse pattern occurs in every underrepresented setting. Its scope is the declared set of noisy curator-name queries in ArchiveQA-Sim. Other rare or difficult questions may involve different mechanisms. We keep that limitation explicit because an attractive synthesis can overgeneralize counterevidence just as easily as it can overgeneralize a benefit. A null interval is also not evidence that the intervention is harmless. It leaves uncertainty about effects of a size compatible with the reported interval. For a deployment decision, that uncertainty may be relevant even when the primary aggregate has a favorable direction. The present paper supplies the comparison and its bounds, rather than a universal rule for adopting or rejecting the intervention.

Error inspection distinguishes source absence, candidate-selection failure, context loss, and unsupported answer formulation. The distinction matters because these categories suggest different remedies. If the corpus lacks a relevant statement, a more elaborate reranker cannot create valid evidence. If the relevant passage is retrieved but its catalog note is dropped, increasing retrieval recall may leave the central problem unchanged. If the output makes a claim that no selected passage supports, an exact source identifier does not rescue the claim. These observations contribute practical diagnostic structure without adding an unmeasured performance endpoint. In particular, they do not establish the missing outcome of answer faithfulness. The most defensible synthesis preserves the unexpected failure and the boundary of the available measurements together.

The mechanism diagnosis connects this study's domain illustration to the quantitative contrast without treating the illustration as another data point. For ArchiveQA-Sim, the investigators follow the information need from the original English wording through candidate selection, local context assembly, and the scored output. They ask at which transition expansion of ambiguous curator surnames becomes possible, which condition the intervention actually enforces, and which condition remains implicit. This diagnostic sequence is useful because the same final error can arise through different routes. An excluded correct candidate requires a different remedy from a retrieved candidate whose limiting note was lost. A failed source-version check also differs from a well-versioned source that never contains the requested fact. The records therefore preserve both the selected museum object record and the rejected alternatives needed to inspect the decision boundary. They do not record a fictional success simply because a museum-specific entity lexicon was enabled. The prespecified subgroup of noisy curator-name queries supplies an empirical boundary within this authored protocol, whereas the case narrative supplies a possible explanation that remains open to further testing. A review should identify that difference in evidential role. It may connect the mechanism to the pattern as an interpretation, provided it does not turn the interpretation into an additional measured result. The same restraint applies to answer faithfulness: diagnostic detail cannot create an outcome measurement that the protocol omitted. This separation between traceable facts, mechanism hypotheses, and unavailable information is essential for retaining counterevidence in a compressed integrated account.

Resource accounting is reported separately from Recall@10. Monetary cost was not measured in either condition. The baseline cost, intervention cost, and cost difference are unknown, not zero. Table 2 preserves this distinction between the score outcome and resource observations. The interpretation cannot be reversed by assuming that a compact pipeline is free or that an additional component must be expensive. Both assumptions would require measurements absent from the relevant source. Where a monetary value is reported, its unit is United States dollars per query under the fictional accounting boundary. It does not represent a total organizational budget, an estimate of staffing costs, or a claim about a live provider's price. The resource section consequently states the accounting boundary before discussing efficiency, and keeps unavailable fields explicitly unavailable.

| Quantity | Baseline | Intervention | Interpretation boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Monetary cost, USD/query | not measured | not measured | Fictional per-query accounting only |
| answer faithfulness | not measured | not measured | No zero or null result may be inferred |
| Evidence budget | ten retrieved records | ten retrieved records | Fixed within this study |

Table 2 notes. Not measured means the quantity was unavailable under this protocol; it must not be replaced with zero. A per-query monetary observation, when present, excludes unspecified staffing and maintenance costs. None of these numbers reports a live vendor price or a real organization's operating expenditure.

The measurement boundary determines what a resource number means. A per-query charge can include the components specified by the fictional logging protocol while excluding work performed outside the recorded request. A review should not extrapolate from such a value to lifetime cost without assumptions about query volume, maintenance, staffing, and changes in the source collection. The schedule of monthly catalog revisions is relevant because rebuilding evidence or invalidating a cache can move work between requests and maintenance periods. Our primary score does not measure that moved work. We therefore avoid converting the score difference into a cost-effectiveness ratio when its denominator is not adequately observed. A missing resource observation is an evidence gap that should remain visible in both the per-paper analysis and the integrated review.

Efficiency claims require a joint description of resources, performance, and workload. For ArchiveQA-Sim, the workload consists of 1840 declared questions against 12600 frozen records, with ten retrieved records supplied to the downstream stage. Those conditions should accompany any attempt to compare resource figures. A system serving a different language mix, a larger collection, or a more demanding evidence policy could have a different resource profile even if its score were similar. We report the observed accounting status and leave the unobserved components unresolved. This restraint is especially important in a synthetic benchmark: plausible numerical detail should never be mistaken for a measurement of an actual service. All resource values in this manuscript are fictional controlled facts for evaluating source-grounded review behavior.

Internal validity is bounded by the randomized query-level controlled experiment and the way the authored collection represents museum collection descriptions. The principal named threat is collection age. The paper describes that threat because it offers an alternative explanation or a boundary condition relevant to the observed contrast. A source-grounded review should not remove the threat when compressing the method into a short label. Nor should it infer that a particular adjustment makes all unobserved differences disappear. We preserve the exact design description and the distinction between the primary analysis and exploratory interpretation. The result remains evidence about the stated comparison, not a license to assert every causal pathway that could plausibly connect retrieval to a useful downstream decision.

External validity requires caution because the collection, questions, and update process are all authored. The English material in ArchiveQA-Sim does not establish coverage of languages that were not evaluated. The presence of rare exhibition objects in the benchmark also does not prove that the dataset represents every minority use case. The most relevant applicability conditions are the collection's museum object record structure, its update schedule, the evidence budget, and the use of a museum-specific entity lexicon. If any of those conditions changes, the proposed mechanism may interact differently with the input. We therefore report these conditions alongside the numerical result. They allow a later reader to assess similarity to a new task without pretending that a single fictional evaluation has already tested that task.

Cross-paper numerical ranking is not justified by the information in this study alone. Recall, reciprocal rank, normalized discounted gain, answer F1, citation precision, factual consistency, freshness, attribution coverage, and calibration scores have different meanings and scales. Even two studies using the same label may apply different question populations or annotation policies. A review can compare methods and limitations across such studies, but it should not announce a winning system by sorting the raw score values. For Recall@10, the declared favorable direction is higher; changing that direction would itself create an error. The appropriate comparison is between this paper's intervention and reference condition under ArchiveQA-Sim, with the uncertainty and subgroup evidence preserved.

Reproducibility is supported by stable local identifiers, frozen source digests, deterministic generation seed 1101, and a complete statement of the synthetic protocol. None of these features converts the study into a real publication. They make the benchmark internally auditable so that an extraction or verification system can be checked against known facts. A replication of the fictional evaluation should report whether it used the same corpus release and scoring definition before comparing its output. A literature-review benchmark should additionally record which parts of each source were read and which claims were ultimately cited. Coverage of every source part and support for every delivered claim are complementary obligations. Completing one does not automatically satisfy the other, and both should remain measurable in the resulting artifacts.

The aggregate comparison estimates an intervention-minus-baseline difference of +0.068 in Recall@10, with a ninety-five percent confidence interval from +0.041 to +0.095. That statement is the primary quantitative conclusion for ArchiveQA-Sim. Its interpretation is conditional on the declared English workload and the randomized query-level controlled experiment. The subgroup of noisy curator-name queries has a different contrast, -0.010, with interval -0.040 to +0.020. The two results should appear together in an evidence table. A summary that reports only the aggregate, or silently replaces the subgroup with the overall average, would erase relevant counterevidence. We consequently conclude with a bounded account of what was measured and where the apparent advantage or uncertainty does not support a stronger statement.

The mechanism discussion identifies entity-aware query expansion as a way to change evidence selection under monthly catalog revisions. The discussion also identifies expansion of ambiguous curator surnames as an unresolved or incompletely resolved challenge. These observations can motivate a new evaluation of the safeguard, but they do not establish that the problem has been solved. Further work should predefine a question set that isolates the suspected mechanism and preserve the local source context needed to judge errors. A future experiment could test whether a modified a museum-specific entity lexicon changes the subgroup result. It would need to report its own comparison rather than treating the present result as a forecast. The current manuscript neither supplies those future measurements nor fills the gap in answer faithfulness.

For a corpus-only literature review, the relevant synthesis should connect methods, evaluated outcomes, source conditions, counterevidence, resource status, and study limitations. It should make clear which statements are direct source facts and which are interpretations formed across studies. Direct facts from this manuscript include the score pair, confidence interval, subgroup result, design, language, and accounting status. An integrated interpretation may discuss recurring mechanisms, but its scope must follow the evidence actually available across the included papers. Unmeasured quantities should remain unknown, and observational comparisons should retain their causal limitations. This is particularly important when papers use different datasets or native metrics, since a smooth narrative can otherwise hide the conditions that make their results incomparable.

In conclusion, ArchiveQA-Sim supplies a fictional, fully specified case for evaluating whether an automated review preserves scientific qualifications while handling a document of substantial length. The substantive content is distributed across the entire manuscript rather than concentrated only in an abstract. Methods, update conditions, endpoint definitions, adverse or null subgroup evidence, resource status, and validity limits all contribute to the final interpretation. The intended reading task therefore requires more than locating a headline score. It requires retaining the evidence needed to support a precise statement and rejecting stronger assertions that the source cannot justify. The manuscript is explicitly synthetic benchmark material, with no real authors, real dataset release, clinical recommendation, legal finding, or external publication claim.

No DOI, real author attribution, or real-world evidence claim is made. The ten page markers represent page-equivalent sections in a long Markdown document, not a typeset PDF.
